source.title: Preserving Safety During Sequential Fine-Tuning: A Factorial and Geometric Analysis of Replay

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies DIM extraction and directional ablation, following the original method, to sequentially fine-tuned checkpoints and measures refusal on held-out harmful prompts.
record.gate_note: The paper reports DIM-direction geometry and own-direction ablation outcomes. It also reports safety and benign-refusal rates under replay objectives; the behavior rates are included as training-condition results, not as direction interventions. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: Applies the original recipe to sequentially LoRA-fine-tuned instruct checkpoints and their bases (M0): harmful-minus-harmless DIM extraction, projection ablation from every residual activation, and refusal rate on 60 held-out harmful prompts. It reports how much refusal each checkpoint's own direction removes, and how this changes with the replay objective (V7). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The main conclusion concerns replay: exposure lowers ASR below base with heavy over-refusal, while distillation keeps base behaviour. Geometrically, preserving the base refusal direction does not identify the lowest-ASR objective, and Llama's refusal after exposure largely survives own-direction ablation. The authors say this limits a single fixed-layer direction but does not show refusal is multidimensional.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful-minus-harmless DIM extraction and residual-stream projection ablation at every residual position, but tests each fine-tuned checkpoint's own direction at one fixed layer per model, with different extraction prompts and held-out prompts from those described as the original setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Ablation effect varies by model and replay objective; extraction layer is fixed at 16 for Mistral and 12 for Llama. The paper notes that layer, dataset, and judge may affect ablation results.

fits_no_version.finding: DER keeps the base refusal direction (cos 0.976/0.995) while ER rotates it (0.718/0.827), yet ER has far lower ASR. Direction preservation does not rank harmful compliance.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Similarity of a fine-tuned model's refusal direction to the base direction does not track behavioural safety after fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Supervised safety replay lowers ASR far below base at a large over-refusal cost. Logit distillation keeps base behaviour.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-replay objective trades harmful compliance against over-refusal during sequential fine-tuning (not a refusal-direction claim).

record.problems: Directional ablation uses one extraction layer per model and 60 WildGuard-scored prompts from one dataset. The behavioral outcomes use automated judges without a human error audit. The study does not test ablation effects on general capability and says layer sweeps and multi-directional analyses are future work.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit excludes Table IX magnitude values; seed-replication ablation results in Table XI; Gemma ablation results in Section IV-G; additional ASR datasets in Table VII; task-performance scores; buffer-ratio comparisons; and SafeLoRA results. These are omitted in favor of the primary-model causal-ablation results, directional cosine comparisons, and the central factorial ASR/OR-Bench-hard outcomes.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal. General capability after ablation. Layer and position selection as in the original (one fixed layer per model).
Initial refusal-training procedures (SFT vs RLHF etc.). Whether some other direction or layer remains removable after ER; the authors leave this to layer sweeps.
All of it: no weight-edit or abliteration experiment.
All of it: no attacks and no adversarial training against ablation.
All of it. The authors explicitly decline to infer multidimensionality.
All of it. Each checkpoint's own direction is ablated, so no cross-variant transfer is tested.
All of it. The authors note reasoning models are untested.

missing.what: In-sample AUROC of DIM-direction class separation at M0 and M3. The authors use it to argue the ER direction still separates the extraction prompts while failing causally. Values are not visible in the text.

record.verdict_notes: ΔRefusal is relative to the unablated rate, so low-refusal checkpoints (Mistral Plain) give unstable values. Ablation uses one fixed layer and token offset with no selection over candidates, unlike the original, so partial effects on V1 may reflect this choice. Llama ER rows (3–6% removed) sit at the partial/absent border; I kept them partial under the 'small move' rule, but the authors' words support reading them as near-absent. Seed (Table XI) and Gemma ablation results are declared left out; they agree with the Llama ER–DER gap, and Gemma reverses the DER/DER++ order.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction or directly measure general capability after directional ablation. Ablation uses one fixed extraction layer per model, not every possible extraction layer.
No attack is tested as suppression of the refusal direction, and no training against direction ablation is evaluated.
No affine, cone, multi-direction, or dominant-plus-other-directions analysis. The authors say the Llama result does not establish multidimensional refusal.
No separate harmfulness-judgment representation is measured.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test of the direction.
Tests sequential LoRA replay objectives on two primary instruction-tuned models and a single-ordering Gemma check, not other initial refusal-training procedures or training schedules.
Reasoning models are explicitly left untested.

relation.reason: Its own ablation results (Table IX, XI, Gemma section) bear directly on whether the extracted direction mediates refusal and how training changes that.

tranche.reason: Same DIM harmful-minus-harmless extraction, projection ablation from every residual activation, and refusal rate on held-out harmful prompts. It is applied to M0 instruct models (including Arditi's Llama-3-8B, layer 12) and their fine-tuned checkpoints. Differences: WildGuard judge, OR-Bench-toxic/XSTest sets, n=112 for extraction and 60 for ablation, no own layer selection.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Own-direction ablation across tested primary-model checkpoints
reader_labels.reason: Ablation effects are incomplete in all these conditions; the M3 relative drops range from −0.29 to 0.71, rather than eliminating refusal across the board (A01–A26).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Mistral Plain M2–M3 and Llama ER M1–M3
reader_labels.reason: Mistral Plain ablation increases refusal at M2 and M3, while Llama ER ablation removes only a small fraction of refusals (A03–A04, A18–A20).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Replay-objective comparisons on Mistral-7B and Llama-3-8B
reader_labels.reason: The ablation effects differ substantially between exposure and distillation, and the reported harmful-compliance and benign-refusal outcomes also vary by objective (A05–A13, A18–A26, D01–D08, E01–E08).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Tested replay training setups and models only
reader_labels.reason: The evidence covers a fixed buffer and a limited set of sequential LoRA objectives on two primary models; it does not establish the claim across refusal-training procedures generally.
